issues.issue: "Damaged cards will be replaced free of charge, but there is a fee to replace a lost card" leaves unclear which rule governs a card that is both lost and later returned damaged. The boundary between "lost" and "damaged" is not defined.

The enumerated privileges (check cashing, elections, athletic events, library, campus technologies) are followed by "etc.", leaving the reach of the catch-all uncertain, and "properly entitled" is nowhere defined. A student and the University could reasonably differ on what falls inside the list.

"Encouraging, enticing, influencing, or enlisting" another student is undefined, and "influencing" in particular has no ascertainable boundary. Ordinary conversation could fall within it on one reading.

"Maintain currency with the use of the University-issued e-mail account" states no frequency or standard, and the following sentence ("communicating information important requests, updates") is garbled by a missing word or punctuation. What the student actually must do is therefore uncertain.

This provision underpins the notice mechanism in Section 19.1 and 19.6 (charges and hearing notice delivered to the Brandeis e-mail account), but it imposes no clear duty that would make such delivery effective notice.

The prohibited behaviours are listed as bare verbs — "intimidates", "threatens", "harasses or bullies", "invades personal privacy", "unwanted physical contact", "endangers the health, safety, or welfare" — with no definitions or intent element. These are the charging standards for discipline and each is reasonably susceptible of narrow and broad readings.

The final sentence permits emergency suspension of any student "involved in such an incident" pending investigation, while Section 22.2 permits altering a student's status only for "reasons of imminent danger". The two cannot easily be read together.

A duty to "comply with instructions of University officials, committees, or boards" is unlimited in subject matter and contains no reasonableness or scope qualifier. Whether it reaches any instruction whatever is genuinely open.
"Dean's Action" is used here as a defined-sounding term but Section 22 speaks of "Dean's Actions and Sanctions" without defining "Dean's Action" as such. The referent is left to inference.

"Obstructing or disrupting ... administrative, public service, disciplinary, or other authorized functions" ends in an open catch-all whose reach beyond the enumerated functions is uncertain. "Legitimate functions" is itself undefined.

"Causes disruption to" and "invades another individual's privacy" are undefined and the sentence's grammar leaves it unclear whether "in a classroom, library or other campus facility" qualifies both verbs. The scope of the prohibition therefore shifts with the reading.

"Issuing any type of threat" is appended to a provision otherwise about safety equipment and is unlimited in scope. Its placement makes it unclear whether it is confined to safety-related threats or free-standing.

The protected categories listed here differ from those listed in Sections 7.0, 7.1 and 7.3 (which add ancestry, religious creed, veteran status categories and "any other category protected by law"). The inconsistent lists leave the covered classes uncertain.

Hazing is "defined" as "initiating or disciplining fellow students, often in the nature of forced alcohol consumption, humiliating or painful ordeals" — the word "often" makes the examples non-limiting so the definition covers any initiation or discipline of a fellow student. The operative boundary of the offense is not ascertainable from the text.

After a list of specific weapons the clause sweeps in "other articles or substances usable as weapons", a catch-all that on its face captures ordinary objects such as kitchen knives or tools. Whether ejusdem generis confines it to weapon-like items is exactly the kind of question a court is asked.

The first sentence bars bringing "any dog or animal" onto campus "without a leash", which read literally requires leashing every animal, while the second sentence exempts guide and service animals only from certain buildings. The two sentences leave the actual rule uncertain.

The host assumes responsibility for "the actions, damage, or injuries caused by" a guest without any limit of foreseeability or fault. Whether this creates strict liability for all guest conduct is genuinely open.

The clause incorporates "regulations enumerated in other official University publications and documents" with only illustrative examples ("e.g."), so the body of incorporated rules is not identified. What documents bind the student is left at large.

The prohibition reaches behaviour that "could be construed as retaliation", a standard defined by how a third party might perceive it rather than by conduct or intent. Its boundary cannot be applied without construction.

The section says non-consensual interaction "could be defined as sexual misconduct or sexual assault" without defining either term, and requires consent to be "sought and clearly understood and communicated" without saying by what measure. This is the charging standard and its terms are left open.

The statement that any student "accused" of sexual misconduct may be placed on emergency suspension pending investigation cannot be squared with Section 22.2, which forbids altering a student's status pending final action except for "imminent danger".

"Sexual misconduct" is prohibited but never defined; the section says only that non-consensual "sexual contact" "may be considered" misconduct, and "sexual contact" is likewise undefined. Whether particular conduct is an offense turns on words the document never fixes.

This section requires "explicit consent" that is "clearly communicated", while Section 3.3 provides that consent "may be communicated verbally or through actions" and may be inferred. The two consent standards point in different directions.

"Taking advantage of someone's incapacitation or intoxication" makes mere intoxication — not incapacity — sufficient, whereas the same sentence treats the two as interchangeable. "Taking advantage of" has no defined content.

Section 3.1 provides that only a student who is "physically or mentally incapacitated" cannot consent, while this section makes sexual activity with a merely "intoxicated" person misconduct. The two provisions set different thresholds.

Lack of consent may be inferred from incapacity "of which the Accused was aware or should have been aware", an objective standard nowhere elaborated, and consent may be shown "through actions". Both formulations are open to competing readings in a disciplinary charge.
Permitting consent to be communicated "through actions" is difficult to reconcile with Section 3.1's requirement of "explicit consent" that is "clearly communicated".

This summary says the Advisor must come "from the University community" and that counsel may give only "passive assistance", but the Advisor definition in Section 22.6 says that where criminal proceedings coexist "the Advisor role may instead be held by a party's attorney". The two descriptions of the right to counsel differ.

"Work that is falsified or is not the result of the student's own effort" is the operative prohibition, and "own effort" is not defined against permitted collaboration or tutoring. The line between a "quality of work" concern and an "integrity" concern is likewise left to the department.

The provision ends mid-sentence ("Talking during an examination, or possession or use of"), so the prohibition it was stating is incomplete. What is forbidden cannot be determined from the text as written.
"Appropriate posting materials that will not cause damage" fixes no standard and is judged only after the fact. A student cannot tell in advance what materials qualify.

The Department may remove chalked messages that are "inappropriate" or use "profane illustrations or language", terms given no content. "Only sidewalks may be chalked" also sits awkwardly against the separate prohibition on areas rain cannot wash.
"Inappropriate use of property" and the extension to "personal and public property that surrounds the campus" have no defined limit. How far beyond campus the section reaches is genuinely uncertain.
"Mistreatment of animals, trees, or plantings" is undefined and covers everything from cruelty to picking a flower. The standard cannot be applied without construction.

The policy prohibits discrimination on the basis of listed categories "or any other category protected by law", an open-ended addition to a specific list whose reach is uncertain. The categories also differ from those enumerated in Sections 2.7 and 7.3.

The "Note" routing all Section 7 allegations to the Special Examiner's Process is difficult to square with Section 19.10.C's "Rights to Fairness" statement, which promises rights (questioning witnesses, presenting witnesses) that the Special Examiner's Process does not provide.

Conduct is "harassment" when it has "the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering" or creates an "intimidating, hostile or offensive environment", judged without any objective-reasonableness anchor. Whether a subjective sense of offense suffices is left open.

The list of sexual-harassment examples is expressly non-exhaustive ("includes, but is not limited to") and prefaced by "Depending on the circumstances", so nothing on the list is necessarily a violation and nothing off it is necessarily permitted. The list's operative effect is uncertain.

The section states the examples are "not an exhaustive list" and then reserves the right to act on conduct the University "deems to be inappropriate, regardless of whether it rises to the level of a violation of law". The prohibited conduct is therefore bounded only by the University's own judgment.

Section 2.14 forbids conduct that "could be construed as retaliation", while this section prohibits retaliation against a person who "in good faith" complains or cooperates. The two formulations of the same prohibition differ in scope.
"Falsified a claim" is not defined and does not distinguish a knowingly false report from an unsubstantiated one. Who makes that determination, and by what standard, is not stated.

"Malicious or unauthorized entry into ... personal files, electronic files ... or locked spaces, such as lockers, etc." ends in an undefined catch-all, and "entry" into electronic files is not explained. The reach of the prohibition is left open.

The section excepts "circumstances as outlined in Section 10.5", a section not reproduced in this instrument, so the scope of the exception to the search-permission requirement cannot be determined from the document.

Reports must be submitted "in a timely manner" and a case may be refused if "not reported in a timely fashion", with no period stated. The limitation period is left entirely to the administrator's judgment.

This section says disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the DSRCS", yet Sections 22.1, 22.3 and 22.4 permit the Dean to remove, suspend or sanction a student without any such report. The word "only" cannot be reconciled with those powers.

The outcome of mediation is said to be "agreed-upon, recorded, final, and binding" while "the Director must also approve all proposed resolutions", so whether the parties or the Director controls the outcome is unclear. "Final and binding" is also unqualified as to further conduct action.

A mediated outcome is described as "final, and binding", but Section 18.2 provides that failure to adhere to it may expose the party to "further mediation or referral to the conduct process". The finality is thus contradicted.

This section allows referral of a defaulting party to the conduct process, which sits against Section 18.1's statement that a mediated resolution is "final, and binding". Whether a mediated outcome forecloses conduct charges is left unresolved.

Failure to choose an option within 2 business days "constitutes an acceptance of responsibility for the violation", a deemed admission with no notice or hardship qualification other than unspecified "extenuating circumstances". The trigger and the escape hatch are both left to the administrator.

The section directs the administrator to "proceed to sanctioning in accordance with Section 19.3", but Section 19.3 addresses only a student's failure to attend a scheduled Administrative Action meeting and prescribes no sanctioning procedure. The cross-reference points nowhere.

The meeting is described as "the only opportunity to present evidence", yet the same sentence says it may be "waived in the event of" the Preliminary Meeting, leaving open whether a student who has had a Preliminary Meeting gets any evidentiary opportunity at all.
"Pending charges may be discontinued thereafter dependent upon the conduct of the Accused" states no criterion and no decision-maker. What conduct produces discontinuance cannot be determined.
The hearing must be held within 30 class days "or as soon as practicable", a qualifier that dissolves the deadline it follows. Whether 30 days is a promise or an aspiration is genuinely open.

The Hearing Administrator is to ensure execution of the hearing "as prescribed in Section 23", but this instrument contains no Section 23 and the hearing procedures are set out in Section 19.10. The governing procedure is mis-identified.

Barring the parties from "confronting or questioning the witnesses and Accusers" before the hearing, while Section 19.6.e makes the parties responsible for notifying their own witnesses of the hearing, leaves the permitted pre-hearing contact uncertain.
Disqualification turns on "good cause" as judged by "the remaining members of the Board", a standard the section does not define. The parties and the Board could reasonably apply it differently.

The section permits the parties to "agree to proceed without the prescribed minimum voting composition of the Board", which duplicates and partly overlaps the waiver mechanism in Section 20.2 requiring consent of the SCB as well. The two waiver rules are not aligned.

The section bars employing "professional legal counsel or other persons from outside the University community" but then allows "passive assistance of legal counsel" where criminal charges coexist, without saying whether such counsel may attend the hearing itself. The right to counsel is left half-stated.

The Advisor definition in Section 22.6 says that where criminal proceedings coexist "the Advisor role may instead be held by a party's attorney", whereas this section prohibits outside counsel from advising the student during the hearing. The two provisions describe the same right differently.

The exception is keyed to "Section 19.16.k", a section that does not exist in this instrument; the intended reference is evidently 19.6.k. The mandatory attendance rule therefore carries a defective exception.

"The right to question all witnesses appearing before the Board and only at the hearing" is grammatically ambiguous: the limitation may qualify the right to question or the witnesses' appearance. The provision also allows written testimony from absentee witnesses who cannot be questioned at all.

This guarantee of a right to view and question all evidence and witnesses has no counterpart in the Special Examiner's Process of Section 22.6, which governs Section 3 and 7 charges and provides for separate interviews with no questioning by the parties.

Placing the burden of proof on the Accuser cannot be squared with the Special Examiner's Process, where a University-appointed Special Examiner investigates and the Dean decides, and no burden is assigned to the Accuser.

A finding of responsibility here requires "clear and convincing evidence", while the Standard of Evaluation in Section 22.6 applies a "preponderance of the evidence" to the same code of conduct. The instrument sets two different burdens for findings of responsibility.

A student who misses a hearing "shall be deemed to have accepted the responsibility", a deemed admission triggered by the Hearing Administrator's own conclusion about fault. The standard for that conclusion is not stated.

Appeals lie "only" on four enumerated grounds, one of which — "denial of rights under this process" — is open-ended, so the closed list is in tension with its own catch-all ground. The scope of reviewable error is therefore uncertain.

This section grants only "the Accused" the right to appeal and promises that a meritorious appeal produces "a new hearing of the case", whereas the Appeals Procedures in Section 22.6 give both parties an appeal that produces only a written report of the UAB's opinions to the Dean. The two appeal regimes cannot be harmonised.

The right to a Dean's review is given only 2 business days from "delivery of the conduct action announcement", while Section 19.7 allows 7 business days to appeal a Board decision. The disparity in review windows for the two tracks is unexplained.

Students "shall ask for a continuance ... rather than wait" to raise new evidence, but the provision does not say that failure to do so forfeits the appeal ground in Section 19.7.d. Whether it is a mandatory bar or advice is unclear.

The heading "Rights to Fairness under this process" introduces five enumerated rights, leaving open whether the list is an exhaustive statement of what fairness requires or merely a script the Chairperson reads. The enumerated specifics sit against a general promise of fairness.

These promised rights — to an Advisor, to present witnesses, to question witnesses appearing against them, to make argument — are unavailable under the Special Examiner's Process of Section 22.6, to which the footnote to Section 19.10 routes all Section 3 and 7 charges. Whether the fairness guarantee extends beyond Board hearings is a genuine internal inconsistency.

This footnote removes Section 3 and 7 cases from the Section 19.10 hearing procedures, and so from the "Rights to Fairness" enumerated in Section 19.10.C, without saying what if anything replaces those rights. Whether the fairness guarantee survives the carve-out is left unresolved.

A not-responsible finding is stated to be "pending approval by the Dean of Student Life or an Associate Dean", although Sections 19.6.i and 21.1 make only sanctions subject to approval and give the Board the decision on responsibility. Whether an acquittal can be withheld is left unclear.

The SCB is denied jurisdiction over "cases related to Sections 3 and 7", yet Sections 22.3 and 22.4 have the SCB advising the Dean on suspensions and sanctions that may arise from the same conduct. The exclusion and those advisory roles are not reconciled.

The voting requirements may be "waived by mutual consent of the SCB, the Accuser, and the Accused", while Section 19.6.c allows the Accused and Accuser alone to agree to proceed without the minimum composition. The two waiver mechanisms require different consents.

"Staff members appointed by the Senior Vice President for Students and Enrollment" is missing its verb ("are"), a slip that leaves the sentence incomplete. The defect is grammatical rather than substantive.

Removal turns on "behavior that conflicts with the high standards of citizenship, confidentiality, and cooperation that the Board represents", a standard with no ascertainable content. It cannot be applied without construction.

This section says the UAB "shall hear appeals of decisions of ... the Special Examiner's Process", but the Section 22.6 Appeals Procedures provide that the UAB only reads written submissions and reports its opinions to the Dean, who retains the discretion to amend or uphold his own decision. The two descriptions of the appellate function conflict.

The UAB is to have "one faculty Chairperson" appointed by the Dean, yet the composition sentence also gives it "two members of the faculty" as voting members while Section 20.7 says an Associate Dean "will serve as Chairperson". The provision does not state whether the Chairperson votes except to break ties.

Section 20.7 provides that "An Associate Dean of Student Life will serve as Chairperson of the University Appeals Board", while this section requires a Chairperson "who is a full-time tenured faculty member" appointed by the Dean. The two cannot both be satisfied.

The factors the decision-maker "may consider" are expressly "including but not limited to", so the enumerated considerations do not confine the discretion at all. "Whenever appropriate" leaves the learning component equally open.

"Sanctions shall not take effect until approved by" the named administrators cannot be reconciled with the Special Examiner's Process, which provides that "[a]ny and all sanctions, including suspension or dismissal, will be in effect immediately, regardless of any appeal". The instrument states two contradictory rules on when sanctions bite.
"Additional conditions may be applied as appropriate" attaches unspecified obligations to what is described as a warning. What may be imposed under a "warning" is undefined.

The privileges that may be lost are "including, but not limited to" a list of specific campus privileges, so the sanction's outer limit is undefined. Whether it could reach academic participation is left open.

A student on probation is subject to further discipline if they "in any way fail to conduct themselves as a responsible member of the University community", a condition with no ascertainable boundary. It is broader than any enumerated code violation.

The sentence "Suspension may extend for a semester, until a designated date, and/or until degrees/certificates will not be issued and credit will not be granted for courses taken elsewhere" is garbled — words are evidently missing after "until". The duration and consequences of a suspension cannot be read from it.

"The University may take any action that it believes to be appropriate and reasonable under the circumstances" on mere "reason to believe" that conduct "may disrupt" safety or well-being confers a power bounded only by the University's own belief. Both the trigger and the permitted response are open-ended.

This unlimited power to alter a student's status is difficult to square with Section 22.2, which provides that pending final action a student's status "shall not be altered" except for reasons of "imminent danger".

The "imminent danger" precondition for altering a student's status pending final action conflicts with Sections 2.1.f and 3.0, which permit emergency suspension of any student merely accused or involved in an incident, and with Section 22.1's power to take "any action" on reason to believe conduct "may disrupt" well-being.

Indefinite suspension may follow a student being merely "charged with" a crime, and the Dean "must consider the nature of the crime and the risk" without any stated standard for the outcome. The provision confers a power whose limits are not stated.

The statement that "[t]he procedural standards set forth in Section 19 do not apply" cannot be squared with Section 22.2, which requires the Section 19.1 procedures to be implemented within 10 class days of any separation from campus.

Off-campus behaviour is sanctionable if "in the judgment of the Dean" it is inconsistent with being a "good citizen and good neighbor" and "adversely affects the University community". These are standards of pure discretion whose content is not fixed by the text.

Excluding the Section 19 procedural standards from "off-campus behavior or Dean's Sanctions" leaves dismissal available with no hearing, which is in tension with Section 18.0's statement that disciplinary action "may be implemented only through the report of a violation to the DSRCS".

The protocol is triggered by "severe emotional or psychological distress" and bars all campus access with "no exception for examinations", yet the section also gives the Dean discretion to "reinstate or restore" privileges. The criteria for either step are unstated.

The promise that "Brandeis is committed to acknowledging and preserving the rights and responsibilities of all its students through all of its disciplinary procedures" sits against a process that withholds the rights guaranteed by Section 19.10.C — an Advisor's active help, presenting and questioning witnesses, a hearing. Whether the commitment is operative or hortatory is a genuine question.

The definition permits an attorney to hold the Advisor role "when co-existing criminal proceedings exist", but simultaneously says the Advisor's role "is passive, and does not include writing or speaking on behalf of their party". What the attorney-Advisor may actually do is left unclear.

Section 19.6.d forbids a party to "employ professional legal counsel or other persons from outside the University community" to advise during a hearing, and the Section 3 services list describes counsel as limited to "passive assistance". This definition instead lets the attorney occupy the Advisor role outright.

The Director decides "in conjunction with the Dean of Student Life" which process applies, whereas Section 22.6 says that a case goes to the Special Examiner's Process whenever "the DSRCS receives a report and determines" a possible Section 3 or 7 violation exists. Whether the routing is discretionary or automatic is unresolved.

The definition does not state who appoints the Special Examiner, what qualifications or independence are required, or whether the Examiner may find facts as opposed to summarising them. The role is described only by what it produces.

The Observer must be "currently or formerly a member of the Student Conduct Board or formerly of the University Appeals Board" — an unexplained asymmetry that excludes sitting UAB members without saying so directly. The eligibility rule reads as a drafting slip.

This definition covers a person with "direct knowledge of the incident", whereas Section 19.6.e defines witnesses as those with "information directly related to the incident in question". The two definitions of the same term do not match.

Making the Dean the renderer of the "Final Decision" is hard to square with Section 20.7, under which the UAB "shall hear appeals of decisions of ... the Special Examiner's Process": the Dean reviews the appeal from his own decision.

Confining the UAB to "a report of its opinions to the Dean of Student Life" contradicts Section 19.7, under which a meritorious appeal requires the UAB to "conduct a new hearing" and permits it to reverse or alter the sanction, and Section 20.7's grant of appellate jurisdiction.

This process applies a "preponderance of the evidence" standard, while Section 19.6.i permits a finding of responsibility for the same code of conduct "based only upon clear and convincing evidence". The instrument sets two different standards of proof.

The 60-day period is framed as a "goal" to be met "or as soon as is practicable if unusual circumstances exist", so whether it is an enforceable commitment or an aspiration is genuinely contestable. "Without unnecessary delay" adds no measurable content.

A failure to cooperate lets the Special Examiner "consider the Accused to have accepted responsibility", and the phase is described as "the principal opportunity" to submit information — neither term is defined, and the deemed admission has no stated threshold. The provision is drafted one-sidedly against the Accused.

The statement that the process "may not be interrupted by the withdrawal from the University by the Accused" conflicts with Section 18.0, which limits discipline to persons "enrolled in any academic program", and with the Note to Section 19.1 permitting deferral when a student is withdrawn.

Evidence "deemed by the Special Examiner to be of material importance" is to be "shared equally with the parties", but the Examiner "retains the discretion not to share certain records". The two sentences leave the parties' access to the record undetermined.
This limited disclosure cannot be squared with Section 19.6.g, which gives the Accused and the Accuser "the right to view and question all evidence and reports presented" to the decision-maker.
Whether any witness is interviewed at all rests wholly on "the discretion of the Special Examiner", with no criterion stated. The sentence also contains the duplicated words "with the the parties".

Section 19.10.C.2 states a party's right "[t]o present witnesses on their own behalf", whereas this provision leaves who is interviewed entirely to the Examiner. The two allocations of control over witnesses differ.

Conducting the parties' interviews "separately" with no opportunity to question the other party cannot be reconciled with the right "[t]o question witnesses appearing against them" stated in Section 19.10.C.3 and Section 19.6.g.
The Examiner need only make "a good-faith effort to contact all pertinent witnesses", and "pertinent" is left to the Examiner's own judgment. The obligation cannot be measured.

The report "summarizes undisputed and disputed facts, and may offer conclusions or recommendations as to the credibility of testimony or potential outcomes" — whether the Examiner may find facts and credibility, or only summarise, is left permissive and unresolved. The Examiner's function is stated in the alternative.

The Dean decides on findings made by another person after separate meetings with each party, which cannot be reconciled with Section 19.6.i's rule that decisions "shall be based solely upon evidence and testimony introduced at the hearing" in the presence of both parties.

The Dean is to render the Final Decision "no earlier than 4 business days, and usually within 7 business days", a mix of a hard floor and a soft ceiling. "Usually" leaves the outer limit unenforceable.

Describing the Dean's decision as "the binding Final Decision" is in tension with the appeal rights in the Section 22.6 Appeals Procedures and in Section 20.7, under which the decision remains subject to review.

Withdrawal of the allegation "will terminate the Special Examiner's Process", yet the University "reserves the right to take actions against the Accused outside of" it, without identifying what actions or under what procedure. The reservation swallows the termination.

An acceptance of responsibility is made "non-reversible" with no provision for withdrawal on grounds of mistake or coercion, and no statement of what disclosure the Accused has had at that point. The finality term is absolute on its face.

The decision is delivered "within 7 days under usual circumstances" and the finding will be "announced" with supporting information merely "referenced", not disclosed. What the Accused is entitled to receive is left indefinite.

Sanctions are those "deemed appropriate by the Dean", whereas Section 21.1 provides that sanctions "shall not take effect until approved by" the Director or a Dean and Section 21.0 frames sanctioning as the province of the DSRCS administrator, the SCB or the UAB. The allocation of sanctioning authority differs between the two sections.

Appeals lie "only" on four grounds, one of which — "denial of rights under this process" — is open-ended, so the closed list is undermined by its own catch-all. What rights exist "under this process" is nowhere enumerated.

The UAB here merely submits "a written report ... of their opinions, thoughts, and suggestions" to the Dean, who "will retain the discretion to amend or uphold the original Final Decision", which contradicts Section 20.7 (the UAB "shall hear appeals") and Section 19.7 (a meritorious appeal produces "a new hearing" with power to reverse or alter the sanction).
